checkpoints: An account owns 3 trust lines and 2 open offers: write the formula for its total reserve requirement.

keyConcepts: Accounts are key pairs (secp256k1 or ed25519); the classic address is a base58check encoding of the account ID.
AccountRoot ledger object stores balance, sequence number, and owned-object count.
Base reserve: minimum XRP every account must hold; owner reserve: additional XRP per owned ledger entry.
Sequence numbers increment by exactly one per applied transaction; gaps or replays are rejected.
Regular keys and signer lists enable delegated and multi-party authorization.
Drops: 1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops, the integer unit fees are quoted in.
labs: Generate an ed25519 and a secp256k1 wallet offline in xrpl.js and compare the resulting classic addresses.

Create one trust line and one offer, then re-query OwnerCount and recompute the account's reserve lockup.
Submit two transactions with the same sequence number; confirm the second fails as a duplicate.
Assign a regular key to a test account and submit a transaction signed only with that key.
objectives: Explain how an XRPL account is defined by its key pair and address.
Compute the total reserve requirement for an account owning N ledger objects.
Predict when a transaction is rejected for a stale or duplicate sequence number.
Distinguish base reserve from owner reserve and their purpose against spam.

checkpoints: What is the difference between a tec-class and a ter-class result for fee accounting?

keyConcepts: Every transaction declares type, Account, Sequence (or TicketSequence), Fee, and LastLedgerSequence.
Signing happens client-side over the canonical binary serialization; the network never sees private keys.
Multi-signing combines weighted signer-list signatures instead of one master-key signature.
Pending transactions sit in each server's transaction queue until consensus validates them.
Ledgers close roughly every 3–5 seconds via the XRPL consensus process and a supermajority of validators.
Transaction results: tesSUCCESS applied; tec/tem/ter classes distinguish claimed-cost failures, malformed, and retryable outcomes.
labs: Build, sign, and submit a Payment in xrpl.js with autofill; log the full signed blob fields.
Submit an identical transaction with a LastLedgerSequence 4 ledgers out; verify it expires unapplied.
Create a signer list on a test account and submit a multi-signed Payment with two signer signatures.
Mint 3 tickets with TicketCreate and use TicketSequence to submit 3 Payments out of order.
Subscribe to the ledger stream and measure the close interval across 20 ledgers.
objectives: Describe the lifecycle of a transaction from signing to validated ledger inclusion.
Choose between single signature, regular key, and multi-signing for a given authorization need.
Set fees and LastLedgerSequence correctly to bound a transaction's retry window.
Use ticket batching to submit sequence-independent transactions in parallel.

checkpoints: Why does a passive offer protect a market maker from being picked off?

keyConcepts: Order books exist per currency-pair; offers are first-class ledger objects, not off-chain intents.
Offers match at quality (exchange rate); tfPassive offers never consume existing offers at a worse rate.
Autobridging routes currency-to-currency trades through XRP order books automatically.
Pathfinding searches trust-line and order-book graphs; Payment paths can combine both.
Partial payments (tfPartialPayment) may deliver less than the requested amount; always check delivered_amount.
Offer expiration and owner reserves make stale-order cleanup an economic design feature.

checkpoints: What happens to existing holder balances when an issuer enables global freeze?

keyConcepts: IOUs exist only where a trust line authorizes a holder to carry an issuer's currency up to a limit.
Trust lines are bilateral ledger objects; limits and quality are set independently per side.
Rippling lets a payment pass through an account's trust lines; NoRipple flags block it.
Issuers can freeze individual trust lines (tfSetFreeze) or enable account-wide freeze (lsfGlobalFreeze).
Authorized trust lines (lsfRequireAuth) let issuers approve holders before balances can be received.
The clawback feature allows issuers to reclaim issued tokens under defined conditions.

keyConcepts: XLS-20 defines the on-ledger non-fungible token standard and its transaction types.
NFTokenMint takes a taxon (issuer-defined grouping/series identifier) and an optional URI.
Transfer fees are set at mint time in basis points up to the protocol maximum and flow to the issuer on secondary sales.
Flags: tfTransferable, tfBurnable, tfOnlyXRP, tfTrustLine control resale, burning, and accepted payment assets.
NFTokenCreateOffer creates buy or sell offers; tfSellOffer marks the direction; brokered mode splits proceeds.
NFTokenAcceptOffer settles a trade; NFTokenCancelOffer and NFTokenBurn complete the lifecycle.

Pools hold exactly two assets and price trades against a constant-product (geometric mean) invariant.
Liquidity providers receive LP tokens proportional to their share; LP tokens are themselves ledger assets.
Single-asset deposits and withdrawals are supported, with slippage handled by the pool math.
A trading fee (capped by protocol) accrues to LPs on every swap.
The auction slot lets one account bid for discounted trading fees for a fixed number of ledgers.
